name: Press-on nails for men

card.summary: Pre-shaped fake nails that glue or stick onto natural nails to give a neat, groomed or styled fingertip look quickly.
card.note: Removal and glue can thin or irritate natural nails.

quick.overview:
Press-on nails are ready-made nail shapes attached to the natural nail with adhesive. For men, they are a quick way to get even, clean-looking nails or to try a painted or styled look without a salon visit or commitment.

The appearance payoff is immediate: uniform shape and colour, or a deliberate fashion statement, that lasts until they are removed.
quick.how: Users choose a size, attach the tip with adhesive and file or shape it. Wikipedia notes press-on tips usually last about 7-10 days, shorter than acrylic or gel.[1] Men who want a subtle effect typically choose short, natural-looking shapes; others use colour or designs.
quick.risks: Reported issues include infection if a nail lifts from the nail bed, thinning from filing and removal, and allergic reactions to some adhesives or gels.[1] Workplaces such as hospitals and food handling often restrict artificial nails.[1]

lead: Press-on nails are a type of artificial nail: pre-made plastic shapes that are glued over the natural nail. They are the simplest and shortest-lasting category of nail enhancement, usually worn for about a week to ten days.[1]

Men use them for quick grooming or for fashion looks, since they avoid the lengthy salon process of acrylic or gel. Artificial nails are historically a status and fashion accessory, from long nails of Ming Dynasty noblewomen to 20th-century acrylics developed from dental materials.[1]
No clinical research addresses their use by men specifically.

chain: Pre-shaped tips cover uneven or bitten nails
Even shape and colour on the fingertips
angle.text: Press-ons give even, uniform nails immediately, either natural-looking or styled, without waiting for growth.

paras: Press-ons are one of several categories: acrylic lasts about three weeks with touch-ups, gel two to three weeks, dip powder about a month, and nail wraps add strength rather than length.[1]

Lifted nails can allow fungal or bacterial infection, filing and removal can thin the natural nail, and some gel products cause allergic reactions when applied improperly.[1] Skin under the free edge can be irritated during filing.[1]

timeline.event: Dentist Fred Slack Jr. creates a temporary artificial nail that leads to the company Patti Nails.[1]
